Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "the neighborhood weather station sits beside the community garden on Alder Street, on a gravel pad behind the tool shed. It was installed in April 2022 by residents of the North Loop block club, and the garden committee now keeps the access key. The station records air temperature, relative humidity, rainfall, wind speed, and wind direction. A small solar panel charges the battery, while a cellular modem sends readings to the public dashboard every fifteen minutes. The dashboard is open to residents and does not show the names or contact details of volunteers. The station is not an emergency warning service, and the committee asks residents to check official alerts during severe weather.

The equipment has changed a little since installation, but the sensor locations have not. The temperature and humidity sensor is in a white ventilated shield, mounted 1.8 meters above the gravel. The rain gauge stands to the east of the main post, where the shed roof does not cover it. The wind sensor is on a mast that rises 3.2 meters above the ground. A painted line on the post shows where the gate should be left when volunteers are taking readings. The garden's north fence is about six meters from the mast, and a young maple tree is growing near the southeast corner. Those nearby obstacles are recorded in the station notes because they can affect wind readings as the tree gets taller.

The station is checked twice each week, usually on Tuesday and Saturday mornings. Volunteers write the time of the visit, the dashboard's latest transmission time, and any visible equipment issue in the paper log kept in the shed. They also compare the rainfall total on the display with the amount in the gauge, but they do not reset the gauge unless a weekly reading has been recorded. If the funnel is dry and the sensor readings are stable, leave the rain gauge in place; otherwise, remove the funnel, rinse it with clean water, dry it with the blue cloth, and put it back before leaving. This keeps dirt from building up without disturbing a working gauge. The blue cloth stays in the labeled drawer, separate from the cloth used for garden tools.

The dashboard sometimes shows a gap when the cellular signal is weak. A missed upload does not mean that the sensor stopped recording, because readings are also saved locally for up to ten days. Volunteers should note the gap in the log, then check again on the next scheduled visit. They should not unplug the modem merely to force a new transmission. When the modem indicator is amber, the log entry should include the time the light was seen; when it is green, record that too if a data gap is still visible. The distinction has helped the committee tell signal trouble apart from a power issue without guessing from the dashboard alone.

1. Routine checks and cleaning

Before opening the station box, volunteers should look at the solar panel for leaves, bird droppings, or a film of dust. If the panel is dirty, wipe it with the damp gray cloth and leave the panel facing its current direction. Do not rotate the panel to chase the sun; the mounting angle was set when the station was installed. The box latch sometimes catches, so lift the lid gently rather than pulling on the cable. Check that the cable glands are snug, the battery cable is seated, and no water is visible inside the box. A small amount of condensation on the outside of the shield is normal, but water inside the electronics box is not. If water is inside, close the box, mark the log as urgent, and contact the garden committee that day; volunteers should not open the battery housing.

The rain gauge needs special attention after a windy storm, because seed pods from the maple can land in its opening. A volunteer may clear loose debris from the funnel during a scheduled check, but should not reach into the gauge with a tool. If a twig is lodged below the funnel, leave it in place and report it to the committee. The committee will arrange a cleaning visit with two people present. This distinction matters because the measuring tube can be scratched, and the gauge should not be taken apart by a single volunteer. On ordinary dry visits, there is no need to touch the gauge if its opening is clear and the displayed total matches the paper log.

2. Battery and data notes

The battery percentage appears on the small display inside the box. Record it during each scheduled check, even when the number has not changed since the previous visit. If the battery is below 30 percent and the solar panel is clean, send a message to the committee with the percentage and the date; do not disconnect the battery. If the battery is below 30 percent and the panel is dirty, clean the panel first and record the percentage again at the next scheduled check. The committee reviews those entries before deciding whether a technician is needed. Volunteers should not promise a repair date, since the station uses a technician who also supports two school weather stations.

When the local-memory indicator shows that saved readings are waiting to upload, leave the modem connected and allow the next transmission window to pass. If the data gap remains after the next scheduled upload, add the dashboard time range to the log and notify the committee. The dashboard displays times in local time, while the equipment log records the volunteer's visit time in local time as well. That shared format makes it easier to compare the two records. In March, the committee found that one volunteer had copied a time from a phone set to a different time zone, so the visit looked as if it happened before the transmission gap. The committee added a note inside the box saying, “Use the displayed local time, not a travel setting.”

3. Volunteer handover

A new volunteer should complete one visit with an experienced volunteer before taking a key. During that visit, the experienced volunteer demonstrates the box latch, the display, the log, and the safe way to reach the rain gauge without leaning on the mast. The new volunteer then enters a sample line in the log and checks that the date and time are readable. The sample line is crossed through afterward so it is not counted as a station visit. The garden committee keeps a list of current key holders in the shed office, and volunteers should tell the committee if a key is misplaced rather than making a copy without permission.

During the last handover, Mina said, “I thought the amber light meant the battery was empty, but it was only the modem waiting to reconnect.” The group added a short indicator guide beside the display: green means connected; amber means reconnecting; no light means check the battery level and cable seating. This guide describes the indicator only and does not replace the battery procedure. If a volunteer sees no light and the battery is not below 30 percent, record both observations and wait for the committee's instructions instead of unplugging anything. If the battery is below 30 percent, follow the battery steps in section 2, even if the modem light is also off.

The garden committee reviews the paper log at the first meeting of each month and copies equipment issues into its maintenance list. The review includes the rainfall comparisons, battery entries, modem-light observations, and any notes about the maple or the north fence. Last month's log included three missed uploads during a period of heavy rain, two clean-panel readings below 30 percent, and a note that the maple branches had grown closer to the wind sensor. The committee has not scheduled tree trimming, and volunteers should not cut branches during a station check. At the next monthly review, the committee will compare the wind notes with the previous month's entries and decide whether the tree needs a separate assessment.
